extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, dramatsists, and students of poetics/literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plot, character, and the parts of tragedy) according to classical poetics; emphasizes plot construction, unity, magnitude, reversal/recognition, and appropriate choice of protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as first principle / soul of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy: Tragedy is the imitation of an action, and of the agents, mainly with a view to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy's primary evaluative dimension is its plot: an artistically constructed sequence of incidents that imitates an action. Even finely finished speeches or precise character-portraits cannot produce the essential tragic effect if the play lacks a properly constructed plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness / whole (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates an action that is complete and whole and of a certain magnitude: a whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot must neither begin nor end at haphazard but conform to causal principles: a beginning does not follow anything by causal necessity, an end follows other events and has nothing following it, and a middle both follows and is followed. Remove an organic part and the whole is disjointed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / appropriate length
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty depends on magnitude and order; the plot must be of a certain magnitude, comprised within limits that can be easily embraced in one view (memory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too small a piece is confused (seen in an almost imperceptible moment); too vast a piece loses unity for the spectator. Rough practical limit: length that admits a change from bad fortune to good or vice versa in a way perspicuous to the audience. The theatrical time-limits of competitions are separate from artistic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (single action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot, being an imitation of an action, must imitate one action and that a whole: the structural union of the parts must be such that if any one is displaced the whole will be disjointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of plot does not mean unity of the hero—one man's life may contain many incidents that cannot be reduced to one action. Avoid including unrelated adventures which have no probable or necessary connexion to the central action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must represent what may happen (probability/necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the function of the poet to relate what has happened, but what may happen, i.e., what is possible according to the law of probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry expresses the universal (how persons of given character will act), whereas history records particulars. Events in the plot should follow from one another by probability or necessity (propter hoc rather than merely post hoc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epeisodic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Epeisodic plots (where episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence) are the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such episodic structures arise from bad composition or from writers stretching plots to please performers; they break natural continuity and lessen tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are either Simple or Complex. A Simple action is continuous and undergoes change of fortune without Reversal (Peripeteia) or Recognition (Anagnorisis). A Complex action includes Reversal, Recognition, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A perfect tragedy should be arranged on the complex plan because Reversal and Recognition (when well handled) heighten pity and fear and produce the tragic wonder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (Peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change by which a train of action produces the opposite of the effect intended, subject to probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in Oedipus the messenger comes to relieve anxiety but reveals the truth and causes the opposite effect; reversals should arise from the internal structure of the plot, not arbitrary chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best form is coincident with a Reversal (as in Oedipus). Recognition can take many forms (even by inanimate tokens); recognition combined with reversal produces pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal causation of reversal/recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal and Recognition should arise from the internal structure of the plot, so that what follows is the necessary or probable result of what went before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid devices where events happen by mere accident; surprise is most effective when the outcome follows reasonably from preceding actions (gives an air of design rather than pure coincidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Incident
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tragic Incident is a destructive or painful action—death on the stage, bodily agony, wounds and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such incidents are parts of the plot and can contribute to pity and fear, but they should be integrated in the plot's causal structure rather than introduced for spectacle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of protagonist (character type)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should not be a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity, nor a bad man rising to prosperity, nor an utter villain; rather a person 'between' these extremes whose misfortune is brought about not by vice but by some error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a character (e.g., Oedipus, Thyestes) is often renowned and prosperous; his fall through error arouses pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (misfortune of a man like ourselves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single issue / single outcome preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot should be single in its issue rather than double; the change of fortune should preferably be from good to bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-thread plots with opposite catastrophes cater to spectator weakness and give a derive pleasure less truly tragic (more akin to comedy). Stage practice and competition show single-outcome tragedies to be most effective when well represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as second principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Character holds the second place: character reveals moral purpose, showing what kind of things a man chooses or avoids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speeches which do not manifest the speaker's choices or moral purpose are not expressive of character. Character matters, but it serves the action—tragedy is imitation of action, and agents chiefly in relation to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought as third principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances; in poetry it corresponds to where something is proved to be or not to be or a general maxim is enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In oratory this corresponds to rhetoric; older poets made characters speak civic language—thought should arise naturally from circumstances and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction as fourth principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good diction expresses the poet's meaning clearly; novices often attain finish of diction before they can construct the plot—implying diction is necessary but subordinate to plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song and other embellishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Of remaining elements, Song holds the chief place among the embellishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song is an important embellishment but subordinate to plot, character, thought, and diction. Use song to enhance the emotional effect, consistent with the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle / Scenery as least artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery has an emotional attraction of its own but is the least artistic part and is connected least with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacular effects depend more on the stage machinist than the poet; reliance on spectacle to produce pity/fear is inferior to producing those effects through the inner structure of the piece. The ideal is a tale that evokes horror and pity when heard, not only when seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce pity and fear by inner structure, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means, but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece—which is the better way and indicates a superior poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct incidents so that hearing the story (without representation) thrills with horror and melts to pity; avoid using spectacle to create the monstrous rather than the terrible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events should come by surprise yet follow one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are terrible and pitiful are best produced when they come on us by surprise, and the effect is heightened when, at the same time, they follow from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise is most striking where coincidences have an air of design; examples (statue of Mitys) show how incidents that appear to have design produce stronger tragic wonder than mere chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantitative parts (separate parts into which Tragedy is divided) are Prologue, Episode, Exodos, Choric song (Parodos and Stasimon); additional forms: songs of actors and Commos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: Prologos = whole part preceding Parodos; Episode = whole part between complete choric songs; Exodos = whole part with no choric song after it; Parodos = first undivided utterance of Chorus; Stasimon = choric ode without anapaests or trochees; Commos = joint lamentation of chorus and actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of parts into the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts of tragedy mentioned (plot elements and quantitative parts) must be treated as elements of the whole and properly integrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing prologues, episodes, choruses, and exodos, ensure each serves the unity and causal development of the central action rather than being ornamental or episodic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as maker of plots
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet or 'maker' should be the maker of plots rather than of verses; he is a poet because he imitates actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when taking historical subject matter, the poet's primary role is to shape events into a probable, universal imitation. Excellence in verse-making is secondary to success in plot-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate relational context for tragic actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of exciting pity and fear must happen between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent; the strongest effects arise when incidents occur between those near or dear to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an enemy kills an enemy or indifferent persons act, pity is minimal except for the suffering itself; tragedies should exploit relationships (kinship, friendship, enmity) to heighten emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purely moralistic/ didactic outcomes (shock without pity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity merely shocks us and moves neither pity nor fear; the utter villain's downfall satisfies moral sense but elicits neither pity nor fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tragic effect, avoid extremes that produce only moral outrage or mere satisfaction of justice. Aim instead for misfortune that elicits pity and fear through relation to character and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer internal dramatic probability over spectacle-driven effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic effect should be produced by the incidents and their inner structure, not by external spectacular devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more the audience can be moved by the narrated sequence alone (as with the Oedipus story), the more truly artistic the tragedy. Resort to spectacle only when it serves the plot's internal aims.
